1:
The word rendered conflict is agreed on and then applied differently. Barnes notes that it is not the word rendered agony in Luke, though that derives from it, and is elsewhere rendered contention, fight and race; it properly refers to the combats of the public games, and stands here for the anxious care Paul had on their account. Ellicott takes it from the striving of the previous verse, its cognate verb, and, looking to a later verse, refers it especially to striving in prayer. Clarke says much the same, that it implies earnest care joined to the most fervent application to the throne of grace: he agonized with God, and his agony was for them. Robertson renders it literally, how great a contest I am having, an inward contest of anxiety like the care of all the churches. Wesley compresses it to three words: of care, desire, prayer.

What it consisted in is filled out by Gill and Henry. Gill takes it from the labouring of the previous chapter, and says the Colossians were not to think those strivings only for the people to whom Paul personally preached: he means his fervent prayers and wrestlings with God, the conflicts of his own mind over the good of the churches, sometimes hoping, sometimes fearing, sometimes rejoicing and at other times weeping at what he heard, and also his combats with the false apostles. Henry says the care amounted to a conflict, that Paul was in a sort of agony and in constant fear what would become of them, and finds him a follower of his Master, who was in an agony for us and was heard in that he feared. Calvin reads the disclosure as deliberate: Paul declares his affection to gain credit and authority, since we readily believe those known to be desirous of our welfare; and it is no ordinary affection that he was concerned for them when in danger of his own life.

Laodicea draws antiquarian notice. Clarke places it on the borders of Caria, Phrygia and Lydia, first called Diospolis, the city of Jupiter, then Rhoas, named at last from Laodice the wife of Antiochus, and famous for its commerce and the fine black wool of its sheep, with Colosse lying between it and Hierapolis. Barnes makes it the capital of Phrygia and its church the lukewarm church of the Revelation, arguing that the rebuke there shows Paul’s fears well founded and the false teachers too successful. Ellicott groups the three cities of the Lycus valley as one community, probably converted at one time, for which Epaphras felt himself responsible, and observes that while Hierapolis and Laodicea were prominent afterwards Colosse never attained importance and left few and meagre remains. Robertson adds that Hierapolis is undoubtedly included, a few late manuscripts inserting it, and that in those cities the Gnostic harm was beginning.

Whether Paul had ever been there divides them. Clarke grants that the words make it probable he had not, but holds this very improbable since he had passed more than once through the country, and thinks he speaks collectively. Ellicott takes the clause to point at Hierapolis while including Colosse, and observes that if Epaphras had been commissioned by Paul the apostle might indirectly be held the founder there, so that the letter stands midway between the familiarity of those to Corinth and Philippi and the reserve of that to Rome. Henry presses the use: the church was not of Paul’s planting, yet he had as tender a care of it as if it were the only people of his charge, and we may keep up communion by faith and love with those we have never seen. Wesley alone reasons from the verse to the style, that Paul therefore refrains from the appellations Brethren and Beloved. Calvin dissents on the city itself: some assign this Laodicea to Galatia, an inscription he judges incorrect.
2:
The verb rendered knit together is traced by four. Barnes lists its other renderings, compacted, proving, assuredly gathering and instruct, and says it properly means to make to come together; the comfort here is had by solid Christian friendship cemented by love, not by outward profession or speculative faith. Ellicott grants two senses, to knit together and to carry with us in argument, that is to convince, but finds the usage of this letter and of the Ephesian one, with the added words in love, decisive for the first. Robertson agrees and calls love the bond that binds all together. Clarke gives the picture: the word signifies being united as the beams of a building are, by mortices and pins, and the visible Church cannot be in union with God unless it have unity in itself, which without love is impossible.

On the full assurance of understanding Barnes is lexical, that the word means firm persuasion and settled conviction and is rendered assurance in every instance. Calvin makes it the mark dividing faith from opinion: a man truly knows the Lord who does not waver in doubt but stands fast in a firm and constant persuasion, and this constancy can no more be separated from faith than heat or light from the sun; the doctrine of the schoolmen he calls devilish, since it takes assurance away. Ellicott turns it the other way and makes love the road to knowledge, since in all personal knowledge he knows best who loves best. Robertson reads the word for full knowledge as Paul’s reply to the Gnostics and their perverted knowledge, and says the verse calls for the balanced exercise of all one’s mental powers. Wesley states it plainly as the fullest and clearest understanding of the gospel.

Whether the closing words are genuine is disputed. Clarke sets out the many forms the manuscripts, versions and fathers give, of God in Christ, of God who is Christ, of God the Father of Christ and more, and holds that so great a variety leaves the strongest presumption that they are glosses crept into the text and of no authority; Griesbach, he notes, left them out. Barnes reports the same variety and that many critics judge the clause spurious, but sees no evidence against it and thinks the strain of the exhortation demands it. He takes the mystery for what had been concealed about the mode of the divine existence, that God subsists in more persons than one. Ellicott would instead render it the mystery of God, which is Christ, and Robertson reads it the mystery of God, even Christ. Calvin presses it further: God cannot be known otherwise than in Christ, so that all who think they know something of God apart from him contrive an idol, and the verse proves the Son God equally with the Father.

The hidden treasures are read as polemic. Ellicott notes the curious order, that in Christ are all the treasures as hidden treasures, and that the word for hidden was almost technical for teaching given only to the initiated, honourable at first and later a name for the spurious; Paul takes it up from the pretenders to abstruse knowledge, and subordinates their watchword knowledge to the higher gift of wisdom. Robertson makes the same point bluntly: Christ sums up all wisdom and knowledge, and the treasures are there whether the Gnostics have found them or not. Calvin explains why they are called hidden, that they do not glitter with splendour but lie under the contemptible abasement and simplicity of the cross. What the treasures are in is disputed in passing: Clarke refers the phrase to the mystery, Barnes and Robertson to Christ, and Gill allows either, since in Christ dwells the fulness of truth from which ours is derived.
4:
The two words for the danger are pressed hard. Clarke says the first means to deceive by sophistry, where the conclusions appear fairly drawn but the premises are assumed without evidence or simply false, and the unwary are carried away; the second gives the plausible conclusions drawn from such reasoning. He lays the practice at the door of the Gentile philosophers, not exempting Plato and Socrates. Robertson glosses the first as cheating by false reckoning and the second as speech adapted to persuade and then speciously leading astray; the art of persuasion is the height of oratory, but degenerates easily into the flashy deceit Paul disclaimed at Corinth; he remarks how winning champions of error can be with a plausibility that catches the gullible. Ellicott says both occur in Paul only here, and that nothing describes the fabrics of Gnostic speculation more exactly, each step resting on some fancied probability and the whole as artificial as the epicycles of the old astronomy; we see them full grown, Paul saw them in embryo. Barnes calls them the plausible arguments of the Greek sophists and rhetoricians.

Henry takes the danger back a step: Satan spoils souls by beguiling them, for he is the old serpent who beguiled Eve through his subtlety, and could not ruin us if he did not cheat us, nor cheat us but by our own folly. What the apostle means by saying this is answered narrowly and broadly. Gill takes it of everything just said, the conflict, the fear, the desire for fuller knowledge and the claim that all wisdom lies in Christ, urged to show affection and put them on guard. Barnes and Robertson rest the warning on the claim just made for Christ. Calvin makes it a rule: because the contrivances of men have an appearance of wisdom, the pious must be preoccupied with the persuasion that the knowledge of Christ is amply sufficient, which is the key that closes the door against all base errors. Men fell into wicked opinions because, despising the simplicity of the gospel, they aspired higher; once a man has devoted his understanding to Christ, no persuasiveness can turn him aside the breadth of a finger.

How Paul can be present is explained much the same way by all who raise it. Gill treats it as an objection anticipated, owning that the apostle had never been corporeally present while holding that he might be present in another sense. Barnes warns against reading too much in: the word means neither the Holy Spirit nor any inspired sight of them, but what we mean when we say our heart is with someone. Calvin gives the purpose, that the admonition not seem unseasonable from so remote a place, and finds in the praise an exhortation to go on as they had begun. Clarke reads the verse against the grain of the last: such words could hardly be used to perfect strangers, and argue a knowledge of the people founded on personal acquaintance.

Order and stedfastness are heard as soldiers’ words. Ellicott reports that from the days of the ancient Greek interpreters both have been noted as military words, one used of discipline generally and the other of the compact solidity of the phalanx, and suggests the choice may have been prompted by the apostle’s captivity under military guard. Robertson draws it out: the line is unbroken and intact, a few stragglers had gone over to the Gnostics but there had been no panic and no breach, and the second word is the solid part of the line that does stand the attack. Calvin keeps the moral sense, taking order for agreement and regulated morals and discipline, and commending their faith for a constancy without which faith is an empty shadow. Clarke concludes that the church was sound in doctrine and strict in discipline, and adds that the Greek is exceedingly soft and musical.
6:
Two warn against making too much of the particles. Clarke says many lay stress on the words as and so and raise fine heads of discourse from them, which may be proper in itself but was nothing the apostle intended: his meaning is simply that having embraced the doctrine of Christ they should hold it fast. Barnes says the word so is the translators’ addition and rather weakens the sense, and that no stress should be laid on it. Robertson puts the weight on the title, which he says occurs nowhere else in Paul, and reads it as meeting the Gnostic errors at three points: the real humanity of Jesus against the Docetic teachers, the identity of the Christ with that Jesus against the Cerinthian, and his lordship. They were taught right. Chrysostom hears a shrewd appeal, taking hold of them beforehand by their own testimony: we introduce no strange addition, he saith, neither do ye. Ellicott compares the entreaties to Corinth and Galatia not to be turned aside to another Jesus or another gospel. Gill dwells on the receiving, which is believing: faith is the eye that sees Christ and the hand that takes hold of him, receiving him not into the head by notion but into the heart, and a whole Christ in all his offices.

On walking in him Barnes says the word denotes the manner of life, and that they are to live under the view of the Saviour they had at first. Robertson makes it continuous: go on walking, stick to your first lessons. Calvin sets the sure way of the gospel against every other and, with Isaiah, bids them walk in it, holding that the truth once manifested should be to us as a brazen wall against all impostures. Chrysostom alone turns the clause against the error the chapter will name later: He is the Way that leads to the Father, and the Angels are not. Wesley reduces it to three words: the same faith, love and holiness.

The double figure of tree and house is worked out by nearly all. Chrysostom takes rooted for fixed, since what is rooted can never remove, built up for attaining unto Christ in thought, and stablished for holding him as a foundation; the word built, he says, shows that they had fallen down, for faith is a building needing a strong foundation and secure construction. Clarke notes it unusual for the apostle to join a tree to a building, and says the roots are to spread far and wide and deep while the house rises on a foundation already laid. Calvin presses both: a tree with deep roots withstands the assaults of winds and storms, one without them is carried about with every wind of doctrine, and a house without a foundation quickly falls. Gill uses both, making Christ the root from which life and fruitfulness are derived and the sure and only foundation. Ellicott and Robertson find the point in the tenses: they were rooted once for all and are being built up continually.

The thanksgiving is variously used. Ellicott says the metaphor changes again, the cup of faith filled to the full running over in a thanksgiving that expresses both faith and love. Chrysostom asks for more, not simply thanks but thanks with great abundance, more than they had learned, and if possible with much ambition. Calvin makes it a guard against presumption, keeping in mind the source from which faith proceeds, and adds that ingratitude often costs us the light of the gospel. Clarke turns it to encouragement, no limit being set to God’s operations on the soul or to its growth. Robertson concludes that they had therefore no occasion to yield to the blandishments of the Gnostic teachers, and Ellicott recalls that in the Gnostic scheme faith was good enough for beginners while knowledge was the jewel of those going on to perfection.
8:
The verb is a thief’s word. Barnes says our spoil now means to corrupt or decay, but the Greek means to plunder as in war: these teachers would strip them as an invading army robs a country. Clarke traces it to prey and carry away, their goods being the salvation received. Ellicott makes it stronger: to lead away as a spoil, triumph over as a captive, make a slave. Robertson notes the verb is late and rare, found here first, and the participle singular: one outstanding leader was doing most of the damage. Calvin changes the picture to thieves who, unable to carry off the flock by violence, drive away some cattle by fraud, making the Church a sheep-fold whose enclosure is pure doctrine: deviate not a nail’s breadth from it. Gill keeps both figures, robbers of the Gospel treasure and wolves in sheep’s clothing.

What philosophy is condemned is the largest question here. Calvin denies that philosophy as such is meant: Paul condemns what men contrive of themselves when wishing to be wise by their own understanding, the difficulty lying in rejecting not contrivances with nothing to set them off but those that captivate by a false conceit of wisdom. Henry allows a philosophy that exercises our reasonable faculties and leads to the knowledge of God, against one that pleases men’s fancies and hinders their faith. Ellicott divides the warning: against treating Christianity as primarily a philosophy, since it is a life and not a knowledge of abstract principles, though it blesses all true philosophy, as Paul at Athens made it an introduction to the higher wisdom; and against speculation in place of the laborious investigation of facts. Robertson says the word occurs nowhere else in the New Testament and is used because the Gnostics were fond of it; Paul condemns not knowledge but knowledge falsely named.

Where the danger came from is disputed. Barnes finds two sources, Grecian philosophy and Jewish opinion, and refers the tradition to the latter. Clarke makes it almost wholly Jewish: Philo and Josephus use the word of the whole Mosaic institutions, and the Jewish philosophy of the Cabala and the Midrashim deserves the name of vain deceit, even Maimonides being often deplorably empty. Wesley faults it on three counts: it promised happiness and gave none, it rested on the traditions of men such as Zeno and Epicurus rather than solid reason, and it never advanced beyond sensible things. Cyril, far earlier, names three classes: the Greeks draw men away by their smooth tongue, they of the Circumcision by the Scriptures they miserably misinterpret, and the children of heretics disguise with the name of Christ, as with honey, the poisoned arrows of their doctrines.

Robertson says tradition is colourless in itself and may be good or bad, and takes the rudiments for anything in a row, like the alphabet, here the arguments of the Gnostics with their aeons and rules of life. Ellicott hears in the tradition the keynote of our Lord’s condemnation of Pharisaic formalism, and marks the difference from the traditions the apostle honours: those begin in revelation and are freely given to all, these in human speculation and were secretly transmitted to the initiated only. The rudiments belong, he says, to the visible sphere and fit only children. Calvin says Christ is set against the rudiments as much as against the tradition, so that whatever is hatched in man’s brain is not according to Christ, the gospel being corrupted by even a small portion of that leaven. Robertson puts the rule plainly: Christ is the yardstick for measuring philosophy, and the Gnostics had it backwards, measuring Christ by their philosophy. Cyril joins doctrine to practice: doctrines are not acceptable to God apart from good works, nor works accepted that are not perfected with pious doctrines, since there is no profit in knowing the doctrines well and being a vile fornicator.
9:
The word for Godhead is weighed carefully. Barnes says it properly denotes the Divine nature and perfections and occurs nowhere else in the New Testament, and uses it to close two doors: it will not do to say with Crellius that the whole Divine will was in Christ, since the word does not mean the will of God, nor with Socinus that the fulness of Divine knowledge dwelt in him. Not one attribute became incarnate but the whole Deity, and of what mere man or angel could such language be used? Robertson distinguishes this word, the essence of God, from the one at Romans for the quality of God, a distinction kept by Lucian and Plutarch, each word occurring only once in the New Testament.

Bodily is the harder word. Clarke says it signifies truly and really, as against typically and figuratively: there was a symbol of the Divine presence in the tabernacle and the temple, but in the body of Christ the Deity dwelt really and substantially. Wesley says the same: personally, really, substantially. Gill keeps the tabernacle image, making the human nature, a true body and a reasonable soul, the house in which the Godhead dwells, and notes that Philo had already called the Logos the house of God. Ellicott finds almost every word emphatic and explains it from the opponents: horror of everything material led them to deny either the reality of our Lord’s body or its inseparable connection with the Godhead. Robertson names the two denials, the Docetic theory that Jesus had no human body and the Cerinthian separation of the man Jesus from the aeon Christ, and says the fulness dwells now in his glorified humanity. Calvin sets this manifestation against all earlier ones: God has often manifested himself, but in part, and in figures or by power and grace, whereas in Christ he has appeared essentially and communicates himself wholly.

Two explain the choice of the word fulness. Ellicott says that in Gnosticism the word stood for the infinite nature of the Supreme Deity out of which the emanations afterwards called aeons received in various degrees of imperfection, and that Paul probably uses it for that reason; it is not finite but infinitely perfect, so that all may draw from it and leave it unimpaired. Calvin argues from perfection: the doctrines of men are additions to supply a deficiency, and since nothing can be added to Christ, whatever men mix in charges him with imperfection, which sets aside the contrivances of the Papists, who allege that they add nothing.

What being complete means is the sharpest disagreement. Clarke objects to the English word as destroying the connection: the world’s philosophy was empty, there is a fulness in Christ, and the Colossians emptied by that philosophy have now been filled with him. He then denies flatly the notion of a completeness in Christ belonging to a believer still incomplete in himself, calling it too bad a doctrine to exist in the oracles of God. Gill holds very nearly that notion: the words affirm what saints now are, yet not in themselves, for none are perfect in themselves, the work of grace being unfinished, sin dwelling in them and the best of them disclaiming perfection. Calvin steers between, denying that Christ’s perfection is transfused into us and holding only that there are resources in him from which we may be filled. On the headship three look ahead to the angels. Ellicott says it is dwelt on with obvious reference to the worshipping of angels, who are our fellowservants under the same Head; Wesley draws the rule that we ask what we need not from angels but from their head; Calvin says the clause is introduced on account of the angels, who will be ours if we have Christ. Robertson puts it shortly: all rule and authority comes after Christ, whether angels, aeons or kings.
11:
Why circumcision enters at all is explained two ways. Gill takes it as heading off an objection to the perfection just claimed, since these were Gentiles and the Jews thought there could be no perfection without circumcision. Ellicott says the abrupt introduction would be hard to understand but for the Jewish observance mixed with this philosophy at Colosse, and Barnes notes that the Jewish teachers made the literal rite necessary to salvation. On the words made without hands, Ellicott says the phrase is used so constantly of heavenly realities against earthly symbols that it comes to mean simply spiritual; Robertson adds that the negative compound is late and rare.

The words of the sins are doubtful. Clarke reports them absent from many manuscripts, versions and fathers and dropped by Griesbach; Ellicott calls them a gloss added to soften the harshness of the body of the flesh. On that harsher phrase Ellicott is fullest: it is the body so far as it is fleshly in the bad sense, since the body itself is not put off, being part of the true man and the temple of God; and it is called the body of the flesh because the bodily rite touched one member only, in symbolism of one form of purity, while the spiritual circumcision puts away the whole power of the flesh, and not in symbol but in reality. Calvin makes the word body a metaphor for a mass of all vices: as we are encompassed by our bodies, so we are surrounded by an accumulation of vices. Robertson notes that the word for the putting off, as of an old garment, occurs nowhere else and was possibly coined by Paul, who had as much right to mint a Greek compound as anyone.

The burial is read against the practice of baptism. Clarke takes it as alluding to the immersions practised in the case of adults, where the person appeared buried under the water, the emerging answering to the rising on the third day; Gill says the same, immersion being a very significant emblem. Wesley grants that the ancient manner by immersion is manifestly alluded to, but insists that no stress is laid on the age of the baptized or the manner, only on our being risen with Christ, so that if we do not experience this our baptism has not answered the end of its institution. Barnes says the belief is as well shown in one mode as another.

What baptism does divides them further. Robertson denies that the new life is caused by the act, calling that a gross misunderstanding, and sets Paul against the Gnostics and Judaizers, who were sacramentalists: baptism pictures a change already wrought in the heart. Calvin ascribes efficacy to the sign, that it may not fruitlessly signify what does not exist, Christ accomplishing at the same time the mortification it represents. Two reach for Abraham. Calvin raises the objection that Abraham was circumcised spiritually and yet had the sign added, answering that Christ now works that circumcision by baptism. Cyril argues that the likeness of our faith adopts us into the sonship of Abraham, since it is as incredible that a man should rise from the dead as that aged persons should have offspring, and that following on our faith we receive the spiritual seal, circumcised by the Holy Spirit through Baptism, not in the foreskin of the body but in the heart. On the faith itself Ellicott finds this letter stronger than Romans, where the resurrection is a likeness and here a participation. Calvin warns that faith must not wander in a confused contemplation of divine power but fix on the power that raised Christ; Clarke adds that believing is the act of the soul while the power to believe comes from God. Wesley alone marks what is not here: the apostle speaks not of justification at all, but of sanctification altogether.
13:
What the uncircumcision of the flesh means divides them. Calvin allows a proper and a figurative sense but prefers the proper: uncircumcision is the badge of alienation from God, not the cause of death but its token, Scripture being used to denoting the loss of the reality by the loss of the sign, as when Adam was kept from the tree that did not confer life. Wesley takes the figurative sense, calling the phrase a beautiful expression for original sin, so that the readers were doubly dead. Robertson agrees that the word is merely metaphorical, of the alienation which uncircumcision symbolised. Clarke restricts the address to converted heathens, who alone were uncircumcised. Henry divides the death in two, dead in law, as a condemned malefactor is called a dead man, and dead in state, by reason of an unsanctified heart; Gill adds that they had lost the image of God and were like dead men, insensible of their state and helpless in spiritual things.

Who does the quickening is a real difficulty. Ellicott says analogy requires God, yet the later clauses surely require Christ, and, finding an overt change of subject in the parallel, he places one here too, at the words and he hath taken it away; grammatically an anomaly, but such are not uncommon in Paul where the teaching runs high. Robertson settles for God, since the parallel says so expressly and the phrase with him must refer to Christ, though he allows Christ as subject of the taking away. Wesley supplies God the Father.

What the handwriting is has been answered many ways. Gill lists them: the covenant with Adam, the agreement at Sinai, God’s book of remembrance, the book of conscience; and he prefers the ceremonial law, which the apostle goes on to describe. Barnes and Clarke agree, and Calvin argues the point, that every Mosaic ceremony carried an acknowledgment of guilt, washings being evidence of pollution and the worshipper who substituted an innocent animal confessing that he deserved that death; whoever still urges them restores the handwriting to its freshness. Robertson brings the papyri: the word is very common there for a certificate of debt, many surviving examples having been crossed out and so cancelled. Ellicott defines it as the bond exacting payment or penalty in default, and warns that it is the first of those metaphors of debt and satisfaction which later theology multiplied, misleading only when taken for the whole truth rather than a part, since forensic figures represent inner realities imperfectly. Wesley counts three ways of destroying such a bond, blotting out, taking away and tearing, and says the apostle uses all three; the bond was not our sins, which were the debt, but their guilt and cry before God.

How it was blotted draws antiquarian guesses, two of them refused. Clarke points to the curses written in the book and blotted out with the bitter waters, and adds that East India ink may be wiped off parchment with a wet sponge, which he says he has often proved; on nailing he suspects some ancient mode of annulling obligations but cannot recall an instance. Barnes reports an eastern practice of driving a nail through a contract. Ellicott knows the suggestion and rejects it as doubtful and unnecessary, offering instead the title on the cross, itself probably nailed there, which declared the reason of the sufferer’s death as the cancelled curse declares the reason of this one. Robertson likewise denies any allusion to the filing of cancelled accounts, and rests on the perfect tense, which marks the removal permanent, the bond being paid and cancelled and incapable of being presented again. On the words against us Barnes says the ordinances fettered the soul and, confined to one people, would have hindered the spread of religion; Robertson says they were against Jews and Gentiles alike, and contrary to both because neither could keep them.
15:
The verb is the crux. Ellicott says the rendering having spoiled, old as the Latin version, makes everything easy, but the word certainly means having stripped himself, and Paul uses it nowhere else but at the third chapter. Two renderings remain: that Christ stripped the principalities from himself, putting off the condition of earthly life that gave them a grasp on him, which he finds harsh though old Greek commentators took it; or that, having unclothed himself, he made a show of them, which he judges easier. He suggests the object may have been left out on purpose, since it was by stripping himself of all that Christ conquered: becoming a show in absolute humiliation, he made the powers of evil a show in his triumph. Robertson reports the same difficulty, says modern scholars differ radically, and settles for despoil with God as subject, since in the cross God showed his power without aid of angels. Gill knows the unclothed sense and the Syriac reading built on it, but prefers the stripping of their armour.

Who the principalities are is agreed by all but one. Gill makes them the infernal powers of darkness, the accuser who objected the debts of the saints. Barnes makes them ranks of fallen spirits that had invaded the earth and drawn its inhabitants into captivity, whom Christ subdues, recapturing those they had taken. Calvin makes them the devils Scripture represents as accusing us before God, now disarmed, the attestation of our guilt being destroyed. Clarke alone makes them men: the words answer to the emperors and generals taken in battle to grace a victor’s triumph, and it is very likely the apostle means the rulers of the Sanhedrin and the synagogues, who had great authority in making constitutions and explaining traditions; the spread of Christianity in Judea destroyed their power, as Protestantism afterwards destroyed the domination of the pope of Rome.

The triumph is read from Roman usage. Barnes says every term in the verse is military and points to the conqueror who displays the kings he has taken, but insists that nothing on earth is meant, only a victory in view of the whole universe. Clarke keeps to the usage: the conquered are spoiled of their armour and exhibited with contumely to the populace. Ellicott draws it furthest, Christ passing in triumphal majesty up the sacred way to the eternal gates with the powers of evil bound behind his chariot, the apparent triumph of darkness over him being his real triumph over it. Robertson enters one caution: no idea of disgrace is necessarily involved in making a show.

Whether the victory was won in the cross or in Christ is disputed. Calvin grants that the Greek allows in himself, and that most manuscripts point it so, but holds the connection imperatively requires the other, what would be meagre of Christ suiting admirably of the cross. He then makes the cross a triumphal car: though there is nothing in it but curse, the curse was so swallowed up by the power of God that the cross has put on a new nature, and no tribunal is so magnificent, no throne so stately, no chariot so elevated as the gibbet on which Christ subdued death and the devil. Clarke refers the words to Christ rather than the cross, and doubts they are genuine, since the versions and fathers differ so greatly and Griesbach dropped them. Barnes allows either by the cross or by himself; Robertson adds the bond. Wesley reads it of Christ and notes the shape of the paragraph, which begins with him, goes on with him and ends with him. Cyril turns the verse into practice: let us not be ashamed to confess the Crucified, but make the Cross our seal boldly with our fingers on the brow and on everything, since it is the sign of the faithful and the dread of devils.
16:
What the prohibition forbids is agreed. Calvin says to judge here is to hold a man guilty of a crime, or to lay a scruple on his conscience so that he is no longer free; if any mortal assumes the office of judge we need not submit, since Christ, the only competent Judge, sets us free. Barnes says the word means to pronounce sentence, they being answerable to Christ and not to man; Wesley puts it bluntly: regard none who judge you. Gill adds that the judaizing Christians were very censorious, ready to condemn a man as in a state of damnation if he did not keep the law of Moses. Robertson reads the tense as forbidding the habit of such judging, and takes the practices for the ascetic rules of one wing of the Gnostics.

The phrase rendered a holyday produces an open quarrel between two of them. Chrysostom says the apostle wrote of a part of a feast because they did not keep the whole of the old rule, nor keep sabbath with precision, so that the words show the greater part done away; and Paul did not say, do not observe them, but let no man judge you, charging others while showing that these were transgressing. Calvin reports that reading, names Chrysostom for it and calls it a poor interpretation, proposing instead a partition, since those who distinguish days separate one from another, a division suited to the Jews but ceased among Christians.

Whether the sabbath is abolished with the rest divides them four ways. Clarke denies any intimation here that the Sabbath was done away or its moral use superseded, holding the command of perpetual obligation, since no type ceases till the antitype comes; and he adds that it is not clear the apostle refers to the sabbath at all, the plural probably meaning their feasts of weeks. Ellicott takes the opposite view, that Paul gives no hint of the Lord’s Day succeeding as a Christian Sabbath, and that though the Jewish sabbath lingered in the Church with a kind of sacredness, its observance was not of obligation. Barnes holds the plural back from the seventh day, since the word covers all the days of holy rest and especially the opening and close of the great festivals, and denies that the passage proves no holy time to be binding. Calvin keeps days without keeping them holy: we do not observe days as though there were sacredness in them, or as though it were unlawful to labour upon them, but respect is paid to government and order, not to days.

The shadow and the body are handled alike and pressed differently. Robertson puts it in a line, that the body casts the shadow and therefore the shadow belongs to Christ. Barnes says the difference is that between a solid substance and a mere outline, so that the shadow can now be of no value. Henry states the advantage plainly, that they had the shadows and we have the substance. Ellicott finds the spirit of the passage that of the argument running through Hebrews, and distinguishes two ways the apostle treats the law: on its coercive side a schoolmaster, on its ritual side a foreshadowing of the substance, useful before the substance was revealed and worse than useless if trusted afterwards. Calvin says those who still adhere to the shadows judge a man’s appearance from his shadow while they have him before their eyes, and meets the objection that the sacraments also represent an absent Christ: as painters do not at first bring out a likeness in vivid colours but draw rude and obscure lines with charcoal, so the representation of Christ under the law was a first sketch, while in the sacraments it is drawn out to the life.
18:
The first word is a judge’s word. Barnes says it occurs nowhere else in the New Testament and belongs to the prizes of the Grecian games, meaning to give the prize against a man. Clarke and Gill both hear the games in it, Gill adding that the judges sometimes acted the unfair part and defrauded the victors, to whom the apostle likens the false teachers. Calvin makes them runners drawn aside from their course, and warns that all who draw us from the simplicity of Christ cheat us of the prize. Ellicott and Robertson look back to the earlier warning and call this the stronger word: there, let no man arrogate judgment over you; here, let no man use that arrogated judgment to cheat you of your prize, since there is one Judge who has right and is righteous.

On the humility Ellicott is the most searching. The Greek is willing in humility and worship, the idiom meaning delighting in; and this, he notes, is the one place in the New Testament where humility is spoken of with something of the condemnation heathen morality gave it. The reason is that humility is a grace whose essence is unconsciousness, and which, being negative in itself, cannot live except by resting on some more positive quality such as faith or love; consciously cultivated and delighted in, it loses all its grace and turns either to the pride that apes humility or to abject meanness. Barnes reaches the same suspicion by another road: such teachers put on the appearance of great modesty and are the more dangerous for it, since no false teachers are so dangerous as those who assume the aspect of humility. Wesley cuts it short: the humility was pretended, and really sprang from their being puffed up.

Whether angels were worshipped at all is where Clarke breaks with the rest. He takes the words of a man who delights in mortifying his body and walks with the apparent modesty of an angel, affecting superior sanctity to gain disciples, and thinks the apostle alludes to the Essenes, who abstained from all sensual gratifications and affected to live the life of angels on earth; the reading that makes it adoration of angels he judges less likely. The others assume the adoration and explain its motive. Henry says it looked like humility to apply to angels, as though men were unworthy to speak directly to God, but that it is unwarrantable, taking honour due to Christ only and giving it to a creature, and that there was really pride in this seeming humility. Calvin sees the same argument in modern dress among those who preach man’s unworthiness to conclude that mediators must be sought, and answers that Christ humbled himself for the very purpose that miserable sinners might betake themselves directly to him.

The next phrase Robertson traces to the mysteries: the verb means to go in and take possession, and inscriptions use it of an initiate who set foot in and performed the rites, so that Paul quotes the initiates’ own word against them; the word for puffed up comes from a pair of bellows. On the head he says the Gnostics dethroned Christ from his primacy and set him below a long line of aeons, doing it with words of praise, as men do now who teach him as merely the noblest of men. Calvin condemns in one word whatever bears no relation to Christ: let anyone who calls us elsewhere be bidden farewell, though in other respects he were big with heaven and earth, for he is empty and full of wind; and a church that grows without the Head grows monstrous, a humpbacked body that will fall to pieces of itself. Ellicott finds greater anatomical exactness here than in the Ephesian parallel, the joints and bands being articulations and ligaments, the increase here being simply the increase of God.
20:
The premise is taken as granted. Gill says the words express no doubt but a supposition pressed home, since by union with Christ they died in him. Barnes turns it into the question the verse asks: if you are really dead to the world, why act as though you still lived under its principles, which ought no more to influence you than this world influences those in their graves. Robertson keeps the figure of baptism: having come out on the other side of the grave, we are not to behave as if we had not. Calvin says death here means abrogation, but says it more forcibly, since those who died with Christ by regeneration were set free from the ordinances. Ellicott alone enters a qualification: ordinances in their place have their value, as means to an end and as symbols of self-devotion, our Lord’s word that these ought ye to have done and not to leave the others undone being the true teaching; it was exalting them to the first place that was the fatal superstition.

Whose words the three prohibitions are is disputed. Barnes says they are not the apostle’s own but a specimen of how those who enjoined such ordinances pressed the subject, finding their eagerness in the rapid succession of the words, with no connecting particle. Gill says the same, the apostle speaking in the person of the Jewish doctors. Robertson calls them specimens of Gnostic rules and reports that later ascetics took them for Paul’s own instead. Wesley simply supplies the objects: an unclean thing, a forbidden meat, a consecrated vessel.

The order of the three is a real quarrel, both parties finding a gradation. Ellicott says the first and last renderings should be inverted, giving a climax of strictness: handle not the unclean thing, taste it not, touch it not with one of your fingers; and he observes that all the commands are negative, marked by the ascetic preference of spiritual restraint over spiritual energy. Calvin reverses the movement. He objects that the received rendering makes the first word repeat the third, and shows from the Greek writers that the verb can mean to eat. On his reading the apostle is mimicking the growth of such rules: at the outset they forbid so much as partaking; having gained that, they forbid tasting what they do not wish eaten; at length they make it criminal even to touch. Human traditions become a labyrinth in which consciences are more and more entangled, and snares which bind at first and strangle in the end. Robertson notes only that two of the three differ little in meaning.

Where the rules came from is answered from the sects. Gill gives the rabbinic list, not to touch a dead body or a bone or a grave, so that the Pharisees washed on returning from market, and names a treatise of the Misna on what defiles by touching. Clarke matches it with a saying that a Nazarite told twice not to drink and drinking notwithstanding is guilty. Barnes and Robertson both point to the Essenes, Barnes reporting that they ate dry coarse bread and drank only water, that many ate nothing until sunset, and that they washed if touched by anyone outside their sect, and guessing that such a society existed at Colosse; Robertson adds that the Pharisees required ceremonially clean hands for all food. Both also warn against a modern misuse of the words. Barnes says they serve as a motto for the friends of total abstinence and express their position very well, but the apostle meant nothing of the kind, and the passage could be pressed with more plausibility against such societies than for them; Robertson remarks that the prohibition law of his own day needs enlightened instruction to make it effective, and that the Pharisees, Essenes and Gnostics alike made piety hinge on outward observance instead of inward conviction.
22:
Whether the clause about perishing is quoted or the apostle’s own is raised by two and answered alike. Barnes calls the point one of considerable difficulty but judges the words the apostle’s own, thrown in in the rapidity of composition, so that the previous verse stands as the Jewish maxim and this clause as a parenthesis. Ellicott reaches the same verdict from the word itself, which means using up: things used up leave no permanent effect behind. Robertson keeps the literal sense: they are for perishing in the using. Gill allows the words of the ordinances or of the meats, and prefers the meats, which cannot defile a man by their use nor sanctify him by abstinence. Calvin finds two arguments, that these things make religion consist in what is outward and frail and has no connection with the spiritual kingdom of God, and that they come from men and not from God, the second being a thunderbolt against all human traditions, since nothing of human invention binds the conscience.

The word for will worship they take alike and apply differently. Robertson says it occurs nowhere else and was probably coined by Paul on the pattern of a word for voluntary slavery. Calvin explains it as a service men choose for themselves without authority from God, and notes why such traditions please us: anyone will find the first outlines of them in his own brain. Clarke presses it furthest: God will be served in his own way, and to refuse his teaching in order to prefer our own fancies is to light a farthing candle as a substitute for the noonday sun. He then enters a caution the others do not: God prescribes the thing and leaves the time and place to men, so that those abuse the text who call the appointing of times and places for worship will worship.

On the humility and the hardness Calvin counts three colours in this appearance of wisdom: self-invented worship, humility, and no sparing of the body. The second pretends obedience to God and men, so that men refuse no burden however unreasonable; but what is in high esteem among men is often an abomination in the sight of God, and this is a treacherous obedience and a sacrilegious humility that transfers to men the authority of God. Barnes says the same of the fastings and penances, that under all this there lurks often the worst kind of pride, and quotes the line that pride may be pampered while the flesh grows lean. Ellicott adds that the superstition and the false asceticism were likely connected, the second being the condition of the supposed spiritual insight of the first.

The closing words are the hardest in the chapter. Ellicott says our version translates literally and seems to make them the false teachers’ own account of neglecting the body, but that there is a fatal objection, since the apostle would then leave the pretension standing without a word of contradiction, which is almost incredible. He therefore sets not in any honour against the show of wisdom, so that the ordinances are of no value, and prefers, of no real value, tending to the satisfaction of the flesh, abrupt but suiting the indignant terseness of the passage and turning back on the teachers the very charge they brought against others. Wesley states that reading without argument: these things are of no real value before God, and upon the whole do not mortify but satisfy the flesh, indulging our self-will and our desire of being distinguished from others. Robertson reports the words as sharply debated, allows that the preposition may mean against, notes that some have suspected a primitive corruption, and ends on the plain observation that mere rules do not carry us far in human conduct, as every father and mother knows, though family and state and church must have some.
